Added `blueprint/agentic-custom-service/plan-agentic-custom-service.md`: the implementation plan for letting an agent create a latchkey custom service at runtime instead of shipping one as hand-written package data.

The plan covers a new `custom-service` permission request type (domain plus an optional cookie login flow, requested and granted in one user action), a user-created layer under `ServicesCatalog` so a created service appears in the permission dialog, the Permissions tab, the Connectors page and the VPS credential sync, and the propagation work each gateway needs. That layer needs no new file: a custom service has to be written into latchkey's own `registeredServices` regardless, the `custom_` prefix says which entries are ours, and everything else about a service is derivable from its registration -- so `config.json` is the store, and there is no second copy to drift from it.

The plan depends on an unreleased latchkey: through 3.8.0 a running gateway loads `registeredServices` once at startup, so a newly registered service stayed invisible until a restart. The latchkey `refresh-services` branch rebuilds the registry per request, which removes the restart from this design entirely; the plan records that the four latchkey version pins must move to the release carrying it before this can merge. One latchkey constraint remains: a registered service with no stored credentials is a hard 400, so a domain with no auth at all stays unsupported.

The agent supplies no display text: a custom service is labelled by its domain everywhere it is named, so the rationale is the only agent-authored string the approval dialog shows, and it reads as the agent's claim rather than the app's description. The grant uses detent's builtin catch-all permission `any` rather than a per-service `everything` schema, so a custom service contributes only its scope schema to the shared schemas file.

The latchkey service name for a custom service is `custom_` plus the domain with dots written as underscores (`a.b.com` -> `custom_a_b_com`). The prefix keeps custom services out of the namespace latchkey's own builtins occupy. The requirement on the substitution is injectivity, not reversibility: nothing ever decodes a name back to a domain (the domain is a field on the stored entry), but two domains must never produce one name -- which the obvious dots-to-hyphens fails, colliding `a-b.com` with `a.b.com`. Because the accepted domain grammar admits no underscore, substituting one is injective.

The plan splits into two changes, because adding a third service source naively would have meant merging a second catalog in two languages at two different times. Bundled additional services are folded into `services.json` at build time by `generate_services_json.py`, while a custom service can only be folded at runtime -- and separately for Python and for the gateway extensions. So the plan first introduces one assembly layer (`service_definitions.py`) that holds all three sources and owns the projections to the catalog, the detent schemas and the `registeredServices` entries, with the generator reduced to emitting detent builtins only. That refactor is behavior-preserving -- with no custom services the materialized `services.json` must equal today's generated file -- it leaves the gateway extensions untouched, and it puts the shipped `claude-ai` service on the same code path a custom service uses. The feature then adds one source to one function.

The bundled `claude-ai` stays bundled. Converting it into a custom service would rename it and its scope and replace its `everything` permission with `any`, and existing hosts carry rules that `$ref` the old scope and name the old permission -- an unresolvable reference fails detent's whole check, so that rename would break every permission on any host that had granted claude.ai, not just its claude.ai access. Existing workspaces therefore need no migration and get no data-format step: the refactor changes who assembles the catalog, the shared schemas, the materialized extensions copy and the `registeredServices` block, not what is assembled. What the bundled mechanism loses is its monopoly -- reaching a service detent has no schemas for no longer needs a repo edit and a release.
